prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, opening the 10^-18 regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B051 as a single-part prize with Katori and Ye, and I am more settled in it than before. The scientific core is a specific, original, experimentally verified idea: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not shift the clock transition, which lets many atoms be interrogated at once. Lindroth's formulation of the distinct step answers the chair's first question, and I would put exactly that into the citation, not general clock accuracy. The result has been reproduced by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) and compared across continents, so maturity is not in doubt. It opens a door to things we could not see before: centimetre-scale relativistic redshifts, tests of constants and local position invariance, and dark-matter searches. For credit, Katori is the originator of the concept and of the first realization. Ye's contribution is the demonstration that the lattice clock reaches the systematics-controlled 10^-18 regime and the many-body control that made it the benchmark instrument, and I regard that as part of the realization and not merely a later refinement, provided the citation says invention and realization together. I also see no reason to dilute a clean two-name configuration with a second, unrelated part.
statement.case_against: My reservations are unchanged in kind but I can now state them more precisely. First, the lineage: the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize recognised enabling technology and the first optical clocks, so the committee must be able to say in one sentence why the lattice clock is a distinct invention, and the magic-wavelength condition is the only sentence I find convincing. Second, attribution has not been checked against the 2001-2003 originals. Lemonde and others were close to the same idea, and I cannot tell from memory whether Ye's role is invention or the accuracy and stability records that followed. If the archival record shows Ye's contribution is only refinement, then Katori alone, or a different third name, would be more defensible than the pair, and I would want that check before the final ballot. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, but I do not think we should wait for it: the Prize is for the discovery or invention, and verification is already in hand.

responses.point: Lindroth locates the distinct step in simultaneous interrogation of many atoms at the magic wavelength, and argues that cross-continent clock comparisons already provide independent confirmation, so the committee need not wait for the SI second.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I have adopted her wording for my citation. It is the only way to separate this prize from the comb and ion-clock prizes without leaning on accuracy, which is a consequence and not the invention. On waiting, I think the argument is decisive for me: the statutes ask for an original, verified discovery or invention, and a metrological convention is not part of that test. Where I would press her is the priority question she herself leaves open. A colleague with her atomic-physics background can read the 2001-2003 papers more reliably than I can, and I would ask her to say plainly whether Ye's name rests on the invention or on the later records.

responses.point: Kroll treats the lattice clock as the cleanest case of a new measurement capability, but lists Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto and Derevianko as possibly material to attribution and notes that Ye is also credited on the cold-molecule candidate.
responses.response: I share the attribution caution but I read the list differently. Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and Takamoto are, for the most part, the people who carried out the accuracy and comparison measurements that confirmed the idea. That is verification, which is exactly what the prize presupposes, and it is not original invention. Lemonde and Derevianko are the genuine priority question, and that is a matter for the archival check rather than for intuition. His point that Ye appears on another candidate does not matter to me, since the committee judges each part on its own merits. His earlier remark that my NV-centre proposal narrows the prize to the qubit discovery without Lukin is fair, and it is one reason B033 stays only an alternative for me.

responses.point: Johansson describes the credit as Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for pushing accuracy and many-body control, and treats the lineage with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the strongest reservation.
responses.response: I agree that this is the strongest reservation, and I think his description is accurate but also exposes the weak point: if Ye's role is only pushing accuracy, then I should say honestly that the pair is less clean than it looks. My answer is that the many-body control and the demonstration of the 10^-18 systematic budget are experimental steps that changed what the clock was, and the citation should name both invention and realization to reflect that. I also value that he moved to this candidate from his own field, where he has a declared stake, and it reinforces that the support here does not come from sympathy for one community.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs IceCube (Halzen) with the lattice clocks, arguing that two discovery-driven parts in different directions make a stronger prize and that the union is exactly three people.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously and I am not hostile to a two-part prize in principle, but I do not find it persuasive here. The pairing is chosen to fit three names, not because the physics is connected. More importantly, the B009 part still rests on a single credited name for a collaboration of hundreds, and nobody in the first round, including its two advocates, has resolved who conceived the detector, who led the 2013 diffuse-flux analysis, and what DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA contributed. Until an expert report settles that, I would not accept a part whose credit I cannot be absolutely sure of, and I would rather give the clock a clean prize on its own.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, says the B009 credit to Halzen alone cannot be resolved from the supplied information and that a thematic pairing may look like a convenience.
responses.response: I appreciate that he states his own weakness so plainly, together with his professional closeness to the field. I agree with his own two objections and they are the reason I do not join him. If the committee does want to pursue IceCube, I would support his and Danielsson's idea of restricting the citation to the 2013 diffuse flux, and I would support asking for an outside expert report, but I would then treat B009 as something for a later year when the credit can be defended, not as a second half for this one.

responses.point: Eriksson answers my attribution concern by arguing that Kane-Mele preceded the HgTe proposal, so a citation narrowed to the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators fairly reflects the chain and Molenkamp's decisive test.
responses.response: His reply narrows the gap without closing it for me. I accept the chronology, and I accept that the citation can be kept narrow, so B050 remains my strongest alternative and I would not oppose it if the committee prefers it. But the Nobel will asks us to credit the people who did the original work, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what made the HgTe experiment possible. A citation that omits the people who told the experimentalists where to look is a defensible judgement, not settled history, and the 2016 topology prize adds some risk of reading it as a second helping. I would prefer the configuration where the committee does not have to defend an omission it knows about.

uncertainties: Whether the 2001-2003 priority record supports crediting both Katori and Ye as inventors and realizers, or whether Ye's role is mainly later accuracy and many-body records, in which case the pair would have to be reconsidered; I would accept an outside archival check on the original papers.
Whether Lemonde and Derevianko, as originators of related magic-wavelength ideas, are close enough to the invention that a two-name credit is unsafe.
Whether the committee as a whole accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on the strength of the magic-wavelength argument.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission from B050 can be defended, since that remains the strongest alternative if B051 fails on attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict affects B051. I share a department-level affiliation at Chalmers with Goran Johansson, who has disclosed a stake in B038, and I would not recuse myself on any shortlisted candidate. I have long-running exchanges with the Japanese microscopy community (University of Tokyo, Kyushu, Tohoku), but no documented link to Katori or RIKEN, and no link to Ye or JILA. For B033 and B050 I have no known tie to the credited names.
